book.unit_title: Application of physics in other fields

title: Physics and other sciences
competency: Explain how physics relates to chemistry, biology, astronomy and geology.

keywords.def: The study of how matter and electromagnetic radiation interact, by wavelength or frequency.
The point where the whole weight of a body seems to act.
The area under a body that holds it up, such as the space between the feet.
The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹² km.

en.text: Physics and chemistry both study matter and its interaction with energy. Atomic and subatomic physics explains how atoms bond. The physics of heat tells whether a reaction can happen. Spectroscopy, the study of how matter and radiation interact, is a tool both sciences share.

am.text: ፊዚክስና ኬሚስትሪ ሁለቱም ቁስን እና ከኃይል ጋር ያለውን ግንኙነት ያጠናሉ። የአቶም ፊዚክስ አቶሞች እንዴት እንደሚተሳሰሩ ያብራራል።

screens.title: Salt from sea water
screens.ask: You boil salty water until it is dry. Salt stays behind. Which physics idea explains this?
opts: Change of state: water evaporates, salt does not
screens.after:
Heat gives water molecules enough energy to escape as vapour.
Salt has a far higher boiling point, so it stays behind.
This is the physics of heat and change of state, used in chemistry.
screens.best: Change of state: water evaporates, salt does not

screens.title: Physics and chemistry
paras: Physics and chemistry both deal with matter and its interaction with energy.
The rules about atoms used in chemistry are explained by atomic and subatomic physics.
The physics of heat tells whether a reaction can go. It also gives the mixture at equilibrium.

screens.title: Spectroscopy
paras: Spectroscopy studies how matter and electromagnetic radiation interact, by wavelength or frequency.
Most of what we know about atoms and molecules comes from it.
Chemistry is rooted in atomic and molecular physics.

screens.title: Physics tools chemists use
items: Each element absorbs or emits its own wavelengths: its fingerprint.
The pattern of scattered X-rays shows how atoms are arranged in a crystal.
Electric and magnetic fields sort ions by mass.
Shows the energy given out or taken in by a reaction.

screens.title: Where the sciences overlap
sets: Matter, energy and how they interact.
Substances, how they are built and how they change.
Living things and how they work.
overlaps: Uses atomic physics and heat to explain bonds and reactions. Spectroscopy lives here.
Uses mechanics, fluids, sound, electricity and light to explain the body.
Studies the chemical reactions inside living things.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The study of how matter and electromagnetic radiation interact, by wavelength or frequency.

screens.text: Physics and chemistry: which part of physics explains how atoms join by covalent bonds?
screens.why:
A covalent bond is a pair of shared electrons.
Electrons and nuclei are studied by atomic and subatomic physics.
So that branch explains bonding.
Fluid mechanics and acoustics are about fluids and sound, not atoms.
Answer: atomic and subatomic physics.
screens.clue: Bonds are about electrons and nuclei.

screens.text: Physics and chemistry: which chemistry topics rest on physics? Pick all that apply.
screens.why:
Atomic structure: electrons and nuclei, from atomic physics.
Chemical bonds: forces between electrons and nuclei.
Radioactivity: decay of unstable nuclei, from nuclear physics.
Periodic properties: they follow from how electrons are arranged.
So all four rest on atomic and molecular physics.
screens.clue: The book lists many on p.3.

screens.text: History of spectroscopy, true or false: it was developed by physicists and chemists working together.
screens.why:
The book says spectroscopy came from joint work.
Physicists explained how atoms absorb and emit light.
Chemists used it to identify substances.
So the statement is true.

screens.text: Choosing a physics tool: a chemist wants to know which elements are in an unknown powder. The best tool is
screens.why:
Each element absorbs or emits its own set of wavelengths.
These spectral lines act like a fingerprint.
Spectroscopy reads these lines without changing the atoms.
A thermometer gives only temperature, not composition.
Answer: spectroscopy.
screens.clue: Think of fingerprints made of light.

en.text: Physics explains how living things work. A body is stable when its centre of gravity is over its base of support. Soft animals like the earthworm move using Pascal's principle. Our voice is sound from vibrating vocal cords when we breathe out, nerves carry electrical pulses, and light (400–700 nm) drives vision and photosynthesis.

am.text: ፊዚክስ ሕያዋን ፍጡራን እንዴት እንደሚሠሩ ያብራራል፤ የስበት ማዕከል፣ የፓስካል መርህ፣ ድምፅ፣ የነርቭ ኤሌክትሪክ፣ ብርሃን።

screens.title: One foot or two?
screens.ask: Why is it harder to stand on one foot than on two?
opts: The base of support is smaller
You weigh more on one foot
screens.after:
On one foot the base of support is very small.
The centre of gravity slips outside it easily.
Then your weight makes a torque that tips you over.
screens.best: The base of support is smaller

screens.title: Mechanics and the body
paras: A body is stable if its centre of mass is over its base of support.
If the centre of mass moves outside the base, the body tips. Its weight makes a torque.
A wider base and a lower centre of gravity make a body more stable.

screens.title: Fluids, sound, electricity and light
paras: Blood flow uses viscosity, the equation of continuity and turbulent flow.
The earthworm, with no firm skeleton, moves using Pascal's principle.
Vocal cords vibrate as air leaves the lungs: that is your voice.
Neurons send messages as electrical pulses.
Light is the radiation between about 400 nm and 700 nm.

screens.title: Which physics?
items: the eye lens forms an image

screens.title: Stable or not?
screens.text: Tap each case. Think: base of support and centre of gravity.
items: Wider base: the centre of gravity stays over it more easily. More stable.
Tiny base: a small lean moves the centre of gravity outside it. Unstable.
Widest base and lowest centre of gravity. Most stable.
The centre of gravity moves toward the bag. You lean the other way to keep it over your feet.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The point where the whole weight of a body seems to act.
The area under a body that holds it up, such as the space between the feet.

screens.text: Centre of gravity: a person carries a heavy bag in the right hand. To stay balanced, they lean
screens.why:
The bag pulls the combined centre of gravity to the right.
The body is stable only if it stays over the feet.
Leaning left moves the centre of gravity back over the feet.
Answer: to the left.
screens.clue: The load pulls the centre of gravity towards it.

screens.text: Physics of the voice: we produce controlled speech sounds when we
screens.why:
Speech is sound made by vibrating vocal cords.
The cords vibrate when air flows past them.
Air flows out of the lungs as we breathe out.
Answer: breathe out.

screens.text: Fluids in animals: an earthworm moves without legs by using
opts: Pascal's principle in its fluid-filled body
screens.ans: Pascal's principle in its fluid-filled body
screens.why:
An earthworm has no firm skeleton.
Its body segments are filled with fluid.
Muscles squeeze the fluid; the pressure spreads equally everywhere (Pascal's principle).
So each segment gets longer or fatter, and the worm moves.
Answer: Pascal's principle in its fluid-filled body.

screens.text: Stability, true or false: we are more stable lying down than standing.
screens.why:
Stability needs a wide base and a low centre of gravity.
Lying down, the base is the whole body: very wide.
The centre of gravity is also very low.
So the statement is true.

screens.ask: Light and vision: visible light is the radiation from about 400 nm to ___ nm
screens.why:
The book gives visible light as about 400 nm to 700 nm.
400 nm is violet; 700 nm is red.
Answer: 700 nm.
screens.clue: Red light is the long end.

screens.text: Pressure in blood: blood must rise 0.4 m from heart to brain. The pressure needed, p = ρgh ≈ 1060 × 9.8 × 0.4, is about
screens.why:
Formula: p = ρgh.
Substitute: p = 1060 kg/m³ × 9.8 m/s² × 0.4 m.
1060 × 9.8 = 10 388; × 0.4 = 4155 Pa.
Result: p ≈ 4.2 × 10³ Pa (about 31 mmHg).
Trap: 4.2 × 10⁵ Pa comes from a wrong power of ten.

en.text: Astronomers learn about far objects only from the radiation they send. Gravity gives the centripetal force for orbits. Each kind of telescope detects one band of the spectrum. Brightness falls with distance²; a light year is the distance light travels in a year (about 9.46 × 10¹² km). Electrons jumping down emit light, jumping up absorb it. Geologists use waves, magnetism, density and radioactivity to study rocks.

am.text: አስትሮኖመሮች ከሩቅ አካላት የሚመጣውን ጨረር ብቻ ያጠናሉ። የብርሃን ዓመት ብርሃን በአንድ ዓመት የሚጓዘው ርቀት ነው።

screens.title: Too far to visit
screens.ask: Stars are far too far to visit. How do astronomers learn what a star is made of?
screens.after:
We cannot visit stars, but their light reaches us.
Each element leaves its own spectral lines in that light.
So the light tells us what the star is made of.

screens.title: Physics and astronomy
paras: Newton's law of gravitation explains the orbits of moons and planets.
Telescopes detect different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum: radio, infrared, visible, and so on.
Computers turn invisible radiation into "false colour" images.

screens.title: Measuring distance with light
paras: Apparent brightness ∝ true brightness / distance².
This is the inverse square law of apparent brightness.
A light year is the distance light travels in one year.

screens.title: Move a star away
screens.ask: Move the star farther. How bright does it look?
screens.note: Double the distance: 1/4 the brightness, not 1/2.

screens.title: One light year in km
steps: d = c × t, with c = 3 × 10⁵ km/s.

screens.title: Atoms, light and the Earth
paras: An electron falling to a lower orbit emits a photon; jumping up, it absorbs one.
These lines show a star's composition and temperature.
Geologists use force, waves, heat, magnetism and radioactivity to study rocks, often without digging.

screens.title: Electron jumps
items: The electron loses energy. The atom emits a photon: a bright line.
The electron gains energy. The atom absorbs a photon: a dark line.

screens.title: Key words
defs: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 × 10¹² km.

screens.text: Inverse square law: a star moves to twice its distance. Its apparent brightness becomes
screens.why:
Law: brightness ∝ 1/d².
The distance is ×2, so brightness is × 1/2².
1/2² = 1/4.
Trap: 1/2 forgets to square the distance.
Answer: 1/4 as much.

screens.text: Atoms and light: an electron jumps from orbit n = 3 to n = 1. The atom
screens.why:
Orbit n = 1 has lower energy than n = 3.
Falling to lower energy releases the difference.
The energy leaves as a photon of light.
Rule: jump down = emit, jump up = absorb.
Answer: emits a photon.

screens.text: Light year, true or false: a light year is a unit of time.
screens.why:
A light year is how far light travels in one year.
"How far" means it is a distance.
1 light year ≈ 9.46 × 10¹² km.
So the statement is false.

screens.text: Gravity in astronomy: what keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth?
opts: Gravity, acting as the centripetal force
A centrifugal force pushing it out
screens.ans: Gravity, acting as the centripetal force
screens.why:
A body moves in a circle only if a force pulls it to the centre.
That centre-pointing force is the centripetal force.
Here Earth's gravity pulls the Moon toward Earth.
So gravity is the centripetal force.
Trap: "centrifugal force" is not a real force in this picture.
screens.clue: Which force pulls towards the centre?

screens.ask: Distance from light travel time: sunlight takes about 500 s to reach us (c = 3 × 10⁵ km/s). The Sun is about ___ × 10⁸ km away
screens.why:
Formula: d = c × t.
Substitute: d = 3 × 10⁵ km/s × 500 s.
d = 1500 × 10⁵ km = 1.5 × 10⁸ km.
Answer: 1.5.

items.ask: Exercise 1.1, light year: the distance light travels in one year = ___ × 10¹² km
items.why:
Formula: d = c × t, with c = 3 × 10⁵ km/s.
One year: t = 365 × 24 × 3600 s = 3.1536 × 10⁷ s.
d = 3 × 10⁵ × 3.1536 × 10⁷ = 9.46 × 10¹² km.
Trap: using hours or days instead of seconds.
Answer: 9.46.

items.text: Physics in chemistry: how do chemists study particles too small to see?
opts: With instruments based on physics, like spectroscopy
By weighing single atoms by hand
items.ans: With instruments based on physics, like spectroscopy
items.why:
Atoms and molecules are far too small to see or handle.
But radiation and fields interact with them.
Instruments like spectroscopy measure that interaction.
So chemists use physics-based instruments.

items.text: Physics of the eye: how does the eye form an image?
opts: The cornea and lens refract light onto the retina
items.ans: The cornea and lens refract light onto the retina
items.why:
The cornea and lens are curved and transparent.
They refract (bend) light so it meets on the retina.
The retina turns the image into nerve signals.
The eye does not send out light.

test.text: Stability: a body is stable when its centre of gravity is
test.why:
Stability rule: the centre of gravity must be over the base of support.
If it moves outside, the weight makes a tipping torque.
Answer: over its base of support.

Spectroscopy studies how matter and electromagnetic radiation interact.
It measures this by wavelength or frequency.
Answer: how matter and radiation interact.

test.text: Inverse square law: a star at 3 times the distance looks
test.why:
Law: brightness ∝ 1/d².
d is ×3, so brightness is × 1/3².
1/3² = 1/9.
Trap: 1/3 forgets the square.

test.text: Atoms and light: an electron jumps from n = 1 to n = 2. The atom
test.why:
n = 2 has more energy than n = 1.
To go up, the atom must take in energy.
It takes in a photon.
Rule: up = absorb, down = emit.

test.ask: Light-year distance: light travels for 2 years. Distance ≈ ___ × 10¹² km
test.why:
1 light year ≈ 9.46 × 10¹² km.
2 years: d = 2 × 9.46 × 10¹² km.
d = 18.92 × 10¹² km.
Answer: ≈ 18.9.

notes.text: p.6 says centripetal and centrifugal force keep objects in orbit; in an inertial frame only gravity (as the centripetal force) does. Lessons say gravity.
p.4: "Soft-bodied animals … that lack a firm utilize Pascal's principle" is missing the word "skeleton".
The blood-pressure estimate (ρgh ≈ 4.2 kPa) is an added challenge built from Discussion question 1.3 (ii).
